title: Evaluation of Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State, Nigeria (2024–2025)
content:
by Paul Waliaula Wekunda, Oladipo Ogunbode, Zainab Dambazau, Oyeladun Okunromade, Musonda Chikwanda

Introduction

Lassa fever is a priority disease in Nigeria. Periodic evaluation of its surveillance systems is essential to strengthen performance and ensure efficient use of limited public health resources. This study evaluated the Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State, Nigeria.

Methods

The evaluation followed the 2001 CDC guidelines and used a cross-sectional mixed-methods design. We reviewed statewide surveillance data from 2024–2025 and selected respondents from 26 health facilities across 15 of the 18 (83.3%) local government areas (LGAs), as well as from the state surveillance unit and WHO. We assessed the surveillance system’s evolution, structure, and resource availability. We analyzed surveillance data by person, place, and time and audited the data for completeness, errors, outliers, and timeliness. Case investigation forms, laboratory forms, and line lists were reviewed to assess variable usefulness and identify data gaps. Structured questionnaires were administered to 30 stakeholders, including 11 key informant interviews, to assess the system’s usefulness, simplicity, acceptability, timeliness, and representativeness. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically.

Results

Since 1969, the Lassa fever surveillance system has evolved from sporadic paper-based reporting to a coordinated, case-based digital platform. Structurally, the system operates from the community to the national level and relies on human resources, surveillance tools, and physical and digital infrastructure. Between 2024 and 2025, 6,296 suspected Lassa fever cases were reported, of which 461 (7.3%) were confirmed, among which 69 (15.0%) died. Three LGAs, Etsako West (204; 44.3%), Esan West (95; 20.6%), and Esan North-East (79; 17.1%), accounted for 378 (82%) confirmed cases. Cases occurred year-round, with increased frequency between November and April. Data completeness exceeded 95%, while errors and outliers were both below 5%. Timeliness assessment indicated that 88.5% of laboratory results were returned within 48 hours and 91.2% of cases were notified within three days. However, 18.7% of cases presented to facilities later than one week after symptom onset. Overall, the system demonstrated strong performance across the assessed attributes. Key operational challenges included delayed or incomplete laboratory feedback, high clinician workload, reliance on Disease Surveillance and Notification Officers to complete forms, and defective electronic devices. Identified data gaps included an unclear definition of the variable “department,” incomplete documentation of “date of death” and “department,” and the absence of a “cause of death” variable.

Conclusion

The Lassa fever surveillance system in Edo State is simple, acceptable, and effective for case detection and outbreak monitoring. Addressing identified operational and data quality gaps could further strengthen system efficiency, sustainability, and public health impact.
